newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Mobil sees Caspian pipeline hurdles.
newsitem.headline: Mobil sees Caspian pipeline hurdles.

text.p: A senior Mobil official on Friday cast a further shadow on progress by an international group to build an oil pipeline to send Kazakh crude to Western markets via Russia, saying key problems had not been ironed out.

Carl Burnett, president of Mobil Corp unit Mobil Oil Kazakstan Inc, which is a participant in the Caspian Pipeline Consortium and one of its major customers, told Reuters in an interview in the capital Almaty that hurdles remained.
"I would not anticipate to see an exchange of shares, or actual acquisition of shares, on the sixth of December even if there is a signing of a shareholders' agreement," he said.
The consortium, known as CPC, plans to meet on December 6 in Moscow to try to push the deal forward, but other participants have said the delayed, risk-laden deal is far from settled.

"One of the things that has to be clarified is the actual role of Transneft as an operator of the pipeline system, how that will relate to how the tariffs are actually set, the general administration of the thing," Burnett said.
On Tuesday, Russia's state pipeline firm Transneft demanded a bigger cut of the cake, demanding equity in the high-stakes project to send Kazakh oil to market.
"You have a situation here where Transneft is not an equity owner, they are only, if you will, I guess, a sort of contract operator," Burnett said.
Mobil and Chevron Corp are the main customers of CPC, a benchmark energy project in the former Soviet Union that will largely define how Caspian oil gets exported.

CPC aims to build a $1.5 billion pipeline from Mobil's and Chevron's vast Tengiz oil field in western Kazakhstan, with estimated reserves of 6-9 billion barrels of oil, through Chechnya to Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiisk.
Burnett described the Russian government as "supportive" on Russian taxes, another major issue holding up the long and complicated negotiations on the project.
"The sense we have is that everyone wants the thing to work and that we're working through getting problems resolved."

But cautioning about the tangled legal and political questions which still hover above the CPC, he said: "I think people sometimes become too optimistic on how fast you can actually move these things because they are complex."

Companies holding a 50 percent stake in CPC are Chevron, Russia's LUKoil, Mobil, Rosneft, Oman Oil Company, British Gas Plc, Italy's Agip SpA, Kazakhstan's Munaigaz and Oryx Energy Company. Kazakhstan, Oman and Russia hold the remaining 50 percent.

Transneft, as the operator of the pipeline, wants a bigger role in the project and is lobbying Russia's Fuel and Energy Ministry to give it an equity share -- something the current shareholders have said could vastly complicate the deal.

The Tengiz partners are anxious for a dedicated export route out of landlocked Kazakhstan. They now rely on rail, barges and tight capacity in existing Russian pipelines to shift output of 110,000 barrels per day (bpd). Peak output will be 800,000 bpd.
Even when the CPC deal does go ahead, Burnett said the pipeline will not solve all of the former Soviet republic's and foreign investors' crude oil export problems.
"One of the things that has to be realised is the CPC does not solve the export problems for Kazakhstan," he said.
He said the pipeline would be fully utilised immediately by existing fields. Other projects, including Mobil's plan to tap Kazakh reserves in the Caspian, would require more pipelines.

Iranian Parliament Speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, in Almaty on Thursday, proposed another pipeline for Kazakhstan that would go through its own territory -- a proposal that could cheer European oil firms but dismay Washington.
U.S. sanctions against Iran preclude participation by U.S. firms in such a deal, despite it being the shortest route to market.

"It (sanctions) makes it much more difficult, absolutely," Burnett said, but added: "There's always the possibility that by them (non-U.S. companies) moving their crude through Iran it opens up other space for U.S. companies."
